name: Ruy López Steinitz Defense Deferred
summary: The Steinitz Defense Deferred (3...a6 4.Ba4 d6) is a solid Ruy López in which Black adds ...a6 to keep the flexible ...b5 resource.
intro: The Steinitz Defense Deferred arises after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 d6, an improved version of the old direct defence with 3...d6. By first inserting 3...a6 and 4.Ba4, Black keeps the useful ...b5 resource in reserve, ready to gain queenside space and harass the retreating bishop rather than allowing it a comfortable life. The result is a solid and sound setup: Black shores up the e5-pawn and develops quietly behind a modest centre, accepting a little less space in exchange for a durable position. Also known as the Improved Steinitz or the Russian Defence, it is a dependable way to sidestep the sharpest main lines of the Spanish.
line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The defining move order is 3...a6 4.Ba4 and only then 4...d6, which distinguishes this line from the Old Steinitz Defence played immediately with 3...d6. The inserted ...a6 is a genuine improvement: because the bishop has already been forced to a4, Black retains the ...b5 break, which gains space on the queenside and harasses the bishop instead of leaving it unchallenged. Black's plan is unpretentious and reliable, defending the e5-pawn with ...d6 and developing the pieces behind a small but solid pawn centre.

Much of the strategic tension revolves around the ...b5 and Bb3 relationship and the timing of White's central expansion. If White captures on c6 the game takes on an Exchange-style character, with Black gaining the bishop pair at the cost of a slightly compromised pawn structure. Otherwise White prepares c3 and d4 to grab space and challenge Black's restrained centre, while Black completes development with a classical ...Nf6 and ...Be7 or a modern fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7, trading a measure of activity for long-term soundness.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: A principal try is 5.Bxc6+ bxc6 6.d4, when White clarifies the structure early and steers toward Exchange-type positions where Black's bishop pair offsets doubled queenside pawns. Alternatively White plays the classical 5.c3, preparing d4 to build a broad centre in true Ruy López fashion, or the flexible 5.O-O to complete development before committing the centre. Against these Black arranges the pieces solidly, keeping the ...b5 advance and the fianchetto plan available depending on how White proceeds.

The sharpest branch is the Siesta Variation, 5.c3 f5, in which Black strikes at White's centre with an aggressive pawn thrust and invites a double-edged fight far removed from the line's usual calm. Elsewhere Black's choice between a classical development with ...Nf6 and ...Be7 and a modern kingside fianchetto shapes the middlegame, while White's recurring plans are the central advance with d4 and the a4 break to exploit any looseness left by ...b5. Throughout, the deferred Steinitz keeps Black's structure compact and hard to crack.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The defence bears the name of Wilhelm Steinitz, the first World Champion, who championed the solid idea of propping up e5 with ...d6 against the Ruy López. The direct form with 3...d6 was found to grant White an easy initiative, so theory gravitated toward the deferred version, inserting ...a6 and Ba4 first, which was dubbed the Improved Steinitz precisely because it repaired the original's drawbacks. It is also traditionally known as the Russian Defence, a nod to its early adherents.

The line enjoyed its greatest prominence in the early twentieth century as a respected, sturdy alternative to the more combative Morphy systems. Its most colourful chapter is the Siesta Variation with ...f5, which took its name from the 1928 Siesta tournament and was employed there with success by Jose Raul Capablanca, giving the otherwise quiet defence a dash of romance. Today the deferred Steinitz is seen less often at the elite level but remains a sound, low-risk choice that rewards patient, positional play.
